Taking Feedback That Lands Hard

Open this after a review, a critique or a note from someone whose opinion matters, when the words keep replaying. It helps you sit with what was said, sort the useful part from the sting, and decide what, if anything, to change.

Feedback · Work · Self-Esteem · Perfectionism · 8 items · whenever you need it

The checklist

  • Write down what was actually said — Getting the words out of your head and onto paper stops them growing in the retelling.
  • Wait a day before you reply — A first reaction is usually about the sting, not the substance.
  • Underline the one line that stung most — Naming the sharpest part shrinks it to a single sentence you can look at.
  • Separate the facts from the tone — Someone can be right about the work and clumsy about how they said it.
  • Ask about the part you do not understand — A short question turns a verdict back into a conversation.
  • Name the part you would keep — Feedback can be useful in part without being true in whole.
  • Pick one thing to change this week — One small change is a response; a full overhaul is a punishment.
  • Tell one person you trust about it — Saying it out loud to someone kind takes the private weight off.

Use this checklist Free account: tick items off and keep each day's record.

How to use it

Run through it whenever you need it, honestly and without scoring yourself. A checklist is a way of noticing, not a test: an item you cannot tick is information about the day, not a verdict on you. Over a few weeks the pattern of what gets ticked and what does not says more than any single pass.

With a free Theraglee account the checklist remembers each pass, so you can look back. Without one, you can still read it here and keep your own copy.
